title: Worksheet — Motion in a Plane
instructions: Attempt ALL questions. Each question is followed by its mark allocation. Take g = 10 m/s² unless otherwise stated. Show working for subjective and case-based questions. The total marks for this worksheet is 29.

questions.question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and a direction, so it is a vector. The others are scalars.

questions.question: Two perpendicular forces of magnitudes 6 N and 8 N act on a body. The magnitude of the resultant is
On level ground, the range of a projectile is maximum when the launch angle is
questions.explanation: R = u² sin 2θ / g; sin 2θ is maximum at 2θ = 90°, i.e. θ = 45°.

questions.question: A particle moves in a circle of radius 2 m at speed 4 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is
The horizontal velocity of a projectile (no air resistance) stays constant throughout its flight.
questions.explanation: No horizontal force acts, so a_x = 0 and v_x stays at u cos θ throughout.

questions.question: Centripetal force is a new kind of fundamental force, separate from gravity, tension and friction.
questions.explanation: Centripetal force is the NET inward force; its physical origin is one of the existing forces (tension, gravity, friction, normal etc.).

questions.question: The maximum height of a projectile launched at speed u and angle θ is H = ____.
The velocity of A relative to B is given by v_AB = ____.
questions.explanation: Relative velocity is a vector subtraction.

questions.question: A projectile is launched at 30 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Find its time of flight, maximum height, and range. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Apply the standard projectile formulas T, H, R component by component.

questions.question: Explain why uniform circular motion is accelerated motion even though the speed is constant.
questions.answer: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity (a vector), not speed (a scalar). In uniform circular motion the direction of velocity changes continuously, so the velocity vector itself changes — there is a non-zero acceleration (the centripetal acceleration, v²/r, directed toward the centre).
questions.explanation: The key distinction is between speed (scalar) and velocity (vector).

questions.question: Derive expressions for the time of flight, maximum height and horizontal range of a projectile launched at speed u and angle θ above the horizontal on level ground.
questions.answer:
Take launch point as origin, x horizontal in direction of motion, y vertical upward. u_x = u cos θ (constant), u_y = u sin θ (decreasing under gravity). a_x = 0, a_y = −g. So x = u cos θ · t and y = u sin θ · t − (1/2) g t².

Time of flight T: set y = 0 (projectile returns to launch height): u sin θ · t − (1/2) g t² = 0 ⇒ t = 0 or t = 2 u sin θ / g. The non-trivial root is T = 2 u sin θ / g.

Maximum height H: v_y = 0 at apex. Use v_y² = u_y² − 2 g H ⇒ H = u² sin² θ / (2g).

Range R: R = u_x × T = u cos θ × 2 u sin θ / g = u² sin 2θ / g.

Notes: range is maximised at θ = 45° (where sin 2θ = 1); complementary angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A car of mass 1000 kg negotiates a flat (un-banked) circular curve of radius 50 m at a speed of 15 m/s. The coefficient of friction between the tyres and the road is 0.5. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) What centripetal force is required for the car to make this turn?
(ii) What is the maximum friction force the road can supply?
(iii) Can the car make the turn safely? Explain.
(iv) What is the maximum safe speed on this curve?
questions.answer:
(i) F_c = m v² / r = 1000 × 225 / 50 = 4500 N, directed toward the centre.
(ii) f_max = μ m g = 0.5 × 1000 × 10 = 5000 N.
(iii) Yes — required force (4500 N) is less than available friction (5000 N), so the tyres can supply the inward force without skidding.
(iv) v_max = √(μ g r) = √(0.5 × 10 × 50) = √250 ≈ 15.8 m/s. The driver is at 15 m/s, just below this safe limit.
questions.explanation: Case-based questions test whether students can apply the centripetal-force concept to a real situation while keeping track of which physical agent supplies the force.
